classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly supplied increase of two to the last term repeatedly, using the suggested number line if needed.

questions.mappingNote: Going up by twos is repeated addition of positive two, represented by rightward movement.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 continues fixed-step sequences and marks the new terms on a number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Continue a sequence by repeatedly adding two across negative integers.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly supplied decrease of two from negative one, continuing leftward through negative integers.

questions.mappingNote: Going down by twos is repeated subtraction of positive two, represented by leftward movement.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 continues fixed-step sequences and marks the new terms on a number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Continue a sequence by subtracting two through zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Continue the sequence by the stated increase of five; no pattern discovery or choice of method is required.

questions.mappingNote: Going up by fives is repeated addition of positive five, represented by rightward movement.
questions.methodNote: Example 4 continues fixed-step sequences and marks the new terms on a number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Continue a negative-integer sequence by repeatedly adding five.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the integer the same distance from zero on the opposite side.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly apply this definition. The closest supplied skill is locating integers on a number line; no arithmetic operation is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 defines opposite integers as equally distant from zero on opposite sides of the number line and demonstrates both directions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the integer the same distance from zero on the opposite side.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the opposite-of-an-opposite rule, including nested negatives.

questions.mappingNote: Rewriting touching signs is the closest supplied skill for simplifying repeated unary negatives; no addition, multiplication or index laws are assessed.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 defines opposite integers and explicitly demonstrates that the opposite of the opposite returns the starting integer, with -(-2)=2. Apply this rule from the innermost parentheses outward.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the opposite-of-an-opposite rule, including nested negatives.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare four integer pairs, including one opposite-of-an-opposite expression.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c directly assess integer comparison. Part d first uses the opposite-of-an-opposite rule, then compares 2 and 3; integer comparison remains the principal assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 compares integers by their left-to-right positions on a number line. Page 4 explains that the opposite of the opposite is the original integer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare four integer pairs, including one opposite-of-an-opposite expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Read signed Celsius temperatures from four supplied graduated scales.

questions.mappingNote: Interpreting signed temperature is the primary assessed skill; reading a vertical scaled number line is secondary. The authored explanations use the supplied scale, but original prerequisite teaching evidence remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Pages 1–2 establish negative Celsius temperatures and ordered equally spaced integers; page 4 teaches opposites. None demonstrates reading a graduated thermometer, determining a minor interval or interpolating between ticks.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read signed Celsius temperatures from four supplied graduated scales.

classification.difficultyReason: Maintain a signed running total using the supplied left-to-right method; additional terms extend the same direct procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Longer chains assess the same positive-integer operations.
questions.methodNote: Apply the left-to-right method of Example 6d, moving right for addition and left for subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three or four successive operations from left to right.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate money and debt into signed calculations and interpret the balance.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires a signed money sentence followed by interpretation as debt or available money.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 represents debt by a negative balance, spending by subtraction and earnings by addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate money and debt into signed calculations and interpret the balance.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a rise in depth or temperature as adding a positive amount to a negative starting value, then report the result with units.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts transfer that taught signed-position model to a stated rise.
questions.methodNote: The submarine example on page 6 adds the positive rise to the negative starting position.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a rise from a negative depth or temperature by adding a positive integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Select addition and subtraction signs to reach a specified result.

questions.mappingNote: The unknowns are operation signs; all operands are supplied, so the assessed arithmetic remains addition and subtraction of positive integers.
questions.methodNote: Check candidate signs by evaluating from left to right, with addition moving right and subtraction moving left.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select addition and subtraction signs to reach a specified result.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate single additions of positive or negative integers using the directly taught sign rule.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, d, f, g, h, i and k directly apply the negative-addend rule; b, c, e, j and l apply positive addition across or below zero. Both supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Adding a positive integer moves right on the number line. Adding a negative integer is rewritten as subtracting its opposite, then evaluated, as in Example 7 and Example 8(a, b).

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate single additions of positive or negative integers using the directly taught sign rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate single subtractions, usually by replacing subtraction of a negative integer with addition.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 states the subtraction rule; page 10 Example 8c–f demonstrates the rewrite and calculation used in a–h and j–l. Part i uses the positive-integer subtraction method on page 6.
questions.methodNote: Subtract a negative integer by adding its opposite, then evaluate. Subtracting a positive integer moves left on the number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate single subtractions, usually by replacing subtraction of a negative integer with addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-term integer sums and differences, rewriting touching signs where necessary.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 Example 9 directly models three-term calculations. Parts a, d, f, h, i, j, k and l require sign rewriting; b, c, e and g use the positive-integer addition and subtraction established on page 6. Page 9 explains the opposite-number rules.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite addition of a negative as subtraction and subtraction of a negative as addition, then evaluate from left to right.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-term integer sums and differences, rewriting touching signs where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Three direct subtractions of negative integers using the taught opposite-sign rule.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 states the subtraction rule; page 10 Example 8(c–f) demonstrates it for positive and negative starting integers. Each assigned part directly applies that method.
questions.methodNote: Subtract a negative integer by adding its opposite, then evaluate the integer sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Three direct subtractions of negative integers using the taught opposite-sign rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate integer sums and differences, including subtraction of negative integers and consecutive operations.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies positive-integer subtraction; b and c apply Example 8's negative-subtraction rule. Parts d–l combine sequential integer operations, with negative subtraction in g–k, matching Example 9. Neither offered reuse candidate has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Subtracting a positive integer moves left; subtracting a negative integer means adding its opposite. Rewrite touching signs, then evaluate consecutive additions and subtractions from left to right, as in Examples 8 and 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate integer sums and differences, including subtraction of negative integers and consecutive operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a temperature rise across zero using subtraction of a negative integer.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 Example 10 explicitly models a temperature rise by subtracting the initial temperature from the final temperature. Page 9 supplies the subtraction-of-a-negative rule; page 6 explains positive movement along the number line.
questions.methodNote: Calculate the rise as final temperature minus initial temperature, then replace subtraction of a negative integer with addition of its opposite.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a temperature rise across zero using subtraction of a negative integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Read each row's initial and final temperatures and apply final minus initial; the headings scaffold the interpretation and every row uses the same rule.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 Example 10 directly models temperature rise as final minus initial; page 9 supplies the negative-subtraction rule and page 6 supplies directed-number context.
questions.methodNote: Find a temperature rise by subtracting the initial temperature from the final temperature, then rewrite subtraction of a negative as addition of its opposite.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate seven temperature rises by subtracting a negative initial temperature from the final temperature.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the temperature rise across zero, then divide by the heating rate to obtain elapsed time.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed operation is dividing the temperature rise by the heating rate; signed subtraction is the prerequisite step. The rate-method teaching dependency remains unresolved.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 Example 10 calculates a temperature rise as final temperature minus initial temperature and rewrites subtraction of a negative as addition. Pages 6 and 9 support directed-number interpretation and subtraction rules. The supplied pages do not demonstrate converting a temperature rise and a per-minute heating rate into elapsed time.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the temperature rise across zero, then divide by the heating rate to obtain elapsed time.

classification.difficultyReason: Form final minus initial across zero and interpret the negative change as a temperature fall rather than simply giving an unsigned difference.

questions.mappingNote: The question requires constructing the directed subtraction -3 - 11 from the temperature context, then interpreting its negative result as a fall.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 on PDF page 10 calculates temperature change as final temperature minus initial temperature. PDF page 6 explains subtracting a positive integer by moving left along the number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a temperature change by subtracting the initial temperature from the final temperature.

classification.difficultyReason: Subtract signed temperatures in six cases and interpret a negative difference in context.

questions.mappingNote: The six inside-minus-outside calculations directly assess signed subtraction; interpreting a negative difference applies the signed-temperature context.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 explains subtraction of a positive integer on the number line. Page 9 states that subtracting a negative number means adding its opposite. Page 10 Examples 8 and 10 demonstrate rewriting subtraction of negative integers and subtracting signed temperatures.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Subtract signed temperatures in six cases and interpret a negative difference in context.

classification.difficultyReason: Model a negative credit-card balance, further spending and income with a multistep directed number sentence.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is constructing and evaluating a directed number sentence from a financial situation; all monetary givens are retained.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 models debt as a negative balance, spending as subtraction and earnings as addition. Page 10 Example 9 evaluates signed addition and subtraction in successive steps. Apply these methods to the balance, further spending and pay.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a negative credit-card balance, further spending and income with a multistep directed number sentence.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise fifty consecutive subtraction pairs in a long alternating sum.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed arithmetic is integer addition and subtraction. The supplied teaching supports each pair's arithmetic, but does not demonstrate regrouping an alternating subtraction expression into consecutive pairs.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6 and 9 explain signed addition and subtraction using number lines; page 10 demonstrates sequential signed calculations. Page 12 introduces repeated addition of a negative integer. The proposed solution evaluates consecutive subtraction pairs, then combines fifty results of negative one.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise fifty consecutive subtraction pairs in a long alternating sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct products involving small integers, negative one and zero.

questions.mappingNote: The multiplication discussion on pages 12–13 and the sign rules on page 13 directly support all twelve two-factor products.
questions.methodNote: Multiply magnitudes and apply the sign rules: unlike signs give a negative product, two negative factors give a positive product, and a zero factor gives zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct products involving small integers, negative one and zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-factor products by applying integer sign rules at successive steps.

questions.mappingNote: Example 11e–f on page 13 demonstrates the two-stage method for three-factor products. Its part f contains a printed intermediate sign error; the authored solutions retain the negative third factor.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate successive products from left to right, applying the two-factor sign rules at each step.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-factor products by applying integer sign rules at successive steps.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a missing signed factor using a known product and the other factor.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 12–13 establish the multiplication sign rules, and page 14 explicitly connects multiplication statements to inverse division statements. Each response completes one multiplication, without introducing algebraic equation solving.
questions.methodNote: Use known multiplication facts and the product sign rules to determine each missing factor; division expresses the inverse calculation, followed by a multiplication check.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a missing signed factor using a known product and the other factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct integer division in fraction notation using the quotient sign rules.

questions.mappingNote: Every part a–p directly assesses integer division in the fraction notation taught by Example 13. Parts a, d, l, o and p have two negative operands; all other parts have different signs. The inspected page 17 concerns later order-of-operations work and supplies no additional step needed here. None of the supplied reuse candidates matches this complete question.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 states the quotient sign rules and Example 13 evaluates signed divisions written as stacked fractions directly in one equality. Divide the magnitudes and use a positive result for two negative numbers and a negative result for different signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct integer division in fraction notation using the quotient sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a missing divisor from a missing dividend, choose the corresponding inverse calculation, and apply signed multiplication or division.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for a missing divisor or dividend in one division sentence. Inverse operations are the primary assessed skill, with signed multiplication and division supporting the calculation. None of the supplied reuse candidates matches this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–15 relate multiplication and division as inverse operations and give quotient sign rules. Example 12 demonstrates signed division. Page 13 supports signed multiplication for missing dividends; page 17 confirms operation conventions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete single-operation division sentences using integer sign rules and inverse operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Link two signed multiplication or division calculations, recognising that division followed by multiplication must also be evaluated left to right.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts require two operations on integers; part f particularly assesses left-to-right evaluation of division followed by multiplication. The closest most advanced assessed skill is order-of-operations-integers. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Page 13, Example 11, applies product sign rules and evaluates successive products. Pages 14–15 establish division as the inverse of multiplication and give quotient sign rules. Page 17 explicitly requires multiplication and division from left to right; Example 14e–f demonstrates the two-step method used here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive multiplications or divisions of directed numbers, working from left to right.

classification.difficultyReason: Select three operations to satisfy each integer number sentence, evaluating multiplication and division from left to right.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts require selecting multiplication or division signs to complete a number sentence. Integer arithmetic supports the task; the directly assessed decision is completing the number sentence. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete source task.
questions.methodNote: Page 13 establishes integer multiplication signs and successive multiplication. Pages 14–15 relate division to multiplication and establish quotient signs. Page 17 explicitly requires multiplication and division from left to right and demonstrates this in Example 14.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select three operations to satisfy each integer number sentence, evaluating multiplication and division from left to right.

classification.difficultyReason: Select bracket evaluation or multiplication before addition and subtraction, then coordinate product signs and subtraction of a negative.

questions.mappingNote: Example 14 on page 17 demonstrates multiplication before addition/subtraction. Example 15(a) and (d) on page 18 demonstrate bracket evaluation and signed products. These methods apply to all eight parts, with brackets evaluated first in e and the negative subtrahend rewritten in h.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Adding a negative subtracts its opposite; subtracting a negative adds its opposite. Retain successive equalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate short signed-integer expressions using brackets and multiplication before addition and subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a negative base from a minus outside a power, evaluate powers before products, and determine signs from repeated negative factors.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 explicitly contrasts negative bases with external negative signs and Example 14 expands squares into repeated factors. These methods apply directly to a–l; page 13 supplies the product sign rules. Page 18 reinforces evaluating powers before multiplication.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate powers before multiplication. A parenthesised negative base is multiplied by itself; a minus outside the powered brackets is applied after the power. Products of two negatives are positive.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate integer powers, distinguishing a negative base from an external negative sign and applying powers before multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate a negative integer power before one multiplication, including an odd power of negative one.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 distinguishes bracketed negative powers and states that powers precede multiplication. Example 14 demonstrates negative-base powers; page 18 Examples 15 and 16 evaluate powers before subsequent operations. Page 13 supplies the integer multiplication sign rules. These methods apply individually to parts a–h.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate powers before multiplication. A bracketed negative base is included in the power; apply the product sign rules when multiplying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate a negative integer power before one multiplication, including an odd power of negative one.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed integer expressions before multiplication and addition or subtraction, including nested negative signs.

questions.mappingNote: Page 18 Example 15 demonstrates bracket-first evaluation followed by multiplication and addition or subtraction. Page 17 states the operation order; pages 9 and 13 supply the negative-integer operation rules required by these eight expressions.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then multiplication, then addition or subtraction. Rewrite addition or subtraction of a negative using its opposite and apply the integer product sign rules.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed integer expressions before multiplication and addition or subtraction, including nested negative signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive multiplication or division operations from left to right, applying integer sign rules.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess left-to-right evaluation of multiplication and division. Parts a, b and d additionally apply negative-integer sign rules taught on pages 13 and 15.
questions.methodNote: Apply multiplication and division from left to right, using the integer product and quotient sign rules. Page 17 states this order and Example 14(e–f) demonstrates successive multiplication and division; page 18 Example 16(a) reinforces the sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive multiplication or division operations from left to right, applying integer sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of negative integers before multiplication and addition.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts combine powers with integer operations. Page 17 gives the order-of-operations rules and Example 14; page 18 Examples 15 and 16 demonstrate staged evaluation. Page 13 supplies the product-sign rules and page 9 supplies addition of negative integers.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate powers first, multiply from left to right, then add or subtract. Bracketed negative bases have positive even powers and negative odd powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of negative integers before multiplication and addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a purchase cost, subtract it from sales revenue and interpret the negative result as a loss.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 states that multiplication precedes subtraction; pages 17–18 demonstrate evaluating integer expressions in stages. Page 9 supports integer subtraction. This question applies those operations to purchase cost and sales revenue.
questions.methodNote: Calculate the multiplication first, then subtract the purchase cost from the sales revenue and interpret the negative difference in context.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a purchase cost, subtract it from sales revenue and interpret the negative result as a loss.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine repeated deposits with an initial balance, then interpret a withdrawal producing a negative balance.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 explicitly places multiplication before addition and subtraction; pages 17–18 demonstrate integer calculations in successive equality steps. Question 11 applies these operations to a bank balance rather than assessing powers.
questions.methodNote: Multiply to calculate the total deposits before adding the initial balance; subtract the cheque amount and interpret the negative result as money owed.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine repeated deposits with an initial balance, then interpret a withdrawal producing a negative balance.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine sales income, per-pizza costs and a fixed daily cost, interpreting a negative result as a loss.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires a contextual multistep calculation: sales income minus production costs minus the fixed van cost. The final negative result is interpreted as a loss. No algebraic equation solving is needed.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 interprets debt using negative integers; pages 9–10 demonstrate directed-number arithmetic. Pages 17–18 teach brackets and multiplication before addition and subtraction, evaluating expressions in successive steps.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine sales income, per-pizza costs and a fixed daily cost, interpreting a negative result as a loss.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine entry revenue, per-person costs and a fixed cost, then interpret positive or negative balances.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires revenue less show-bag costs and the hall rental. Part c combines two revenue groups while retaining a show bag for every attendee. Multistep contextual operations are the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Represent income minus expenditure as a directed-number calculation. Evaluate multiplication before addition and subtraction, and interpret a negative balance as a loss, following the money interpretations on page 6 and order-of-operations teaching and Examples 14–16 on pages 17–18.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine entry revenue, per-person costs and a fixed cost, then interpret positive or negative balances.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct addition of two integers, including adding negative integers and crossing zero.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly adds two integers. Negative addends are rewritten as subtraction; positive addends increase the starting value. No indices or order-of-operations method is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 teaches adding a positive integer by moving right on a number line. Page 9 teaches adding a negative integer by subtracting its opposite, with negative and positive starting values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct addition of two integers, including adding negative integers and crossing zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate seven wickets into seven five-run deductions, combine this with the runs scored, and evaluate the resulting multiplication and subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses constructing a directed number sentence from the embedded cricket scoring rule, then evaluating its multiplication and subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 models losses by subtraction; pages 9–10 explain directed-number addition and subtraction. Pages 17–18 require multiplication before addition or subtraction and show successive equalities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate the scoring rule into a directed number sentence, multiply the wicket penalty and combine the scores.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the stated maximum and minimum into each explicitly ordered subtraction, then apply subtraction of a negative while preserving the result's sign.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess subtraction of negative integers in a temperature context; no indices or order-of-operations extension is required.
questions.methodNote: Subtract a negative integer by adding its opposite. Page 10 Example 10 models a temperature difference by subtracting the initial negative temperature, rewriting the touching signs, then calculating.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two negative temperatures into explicitly ordered subtractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute two given temperatures and subtract signed integers in each order.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly uses the subtraction-of-a-negative rule shown on page 9. Part b subtracts a positive temperature from a negative temperature, giving a more negative result. Both assess signed-integer subtraction in a temperature context.
questions.methodNote: Subtracting a negative integer means adding its opposite; subtraction of a positive integer moves left on the number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two given temperatures and subtract signed integers in each order.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of two signed integers using the product sign rules.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess the signed multiplication taught on page 13. Parts a, b, c, e, i and j have opposite signs; parts d, f, g, h, k and l have two negative factors.
questions.methodNote: Apply the sign-of-product rules, then multiply the positive magnitudes. Two negative factors give a positive product; opposite signs give a negative product. Page 13 explicitly demonstrates these rewrites and evaluates signed products in Example 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of two signed integers using the product sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply signed division rules directly; part i additionally requires an exact non-integral quotient.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess signed division. Parts a, b, c, j and l have different signs; d, e, f, g, h and k have two negative operands. Part i has different signs and additionally requires fraction simplification, whose prerequisite teaching evidence remains missing.
questions.methodNote: Page 15 gives the sign rules for quotients and Examples 12–13 demonstrate direct signed division and fraction notation. Apply these rules and divide magnitudes. The supplied teaching does not demonstrate simplifying a non-integral signed quotient to a mixed number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply signed division rules directly; part i additionally requires an exact non-integral quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate brackets before signed multiplication and distinguish a negative square from its opposite.

questions.mappingNote: Page 18 Example 15a demonstrates bracket evaluation followed by multiplication for a–e and g–i. Page 13 supplies signed-product rules. Page 17 distinguishes squares of negative numbers from taking the opposite of a square, supporting f. Pages 9 and 15 supply signed addition and division context; division is not assessed here.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then powers, then multiplication. Apply the signed-product rules. For f, square the bracketed negative number before taking its opposite.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate brackets before signed multiplication and distinguish a negative square from its opposite.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate an ordered verbal calculation into signed addition, subtraction and multiplication.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 supports signed addition and subtraction; page 13 supplies the negative-times-positive rule. Pages 17–18 demonstrate bracketed integer calculations and stepwise evaluation. Page 15 was inspected but its division method is not needed.
questions.methodNote: Perform the stated additions and subtraction first, then multiply the resulting negative integer by a positive integer. Brackets preserve the verbal operation order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate an ordered verbal calculation into signed addition, subtraction and multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow a stated sequence of subtraction, addition of a negative integer and division.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 supplies the negative-addition rule, page 15 supplies signed division, and pages 17–18 demonstrate ordered evaluation with brackets and complete intermediate calculations. The question explicitly requires division after the preceding additions and subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Add a negative integer by subtracting its opposite; evaluate the accumulated result before dividing. A negative integer divided by a positive integer gives a negative quotient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow a stated sequence of subtraction, addition of a negative integer and division.
